summary: Explain token-slicing and dynamic refill impact on mixed streaming + bulk traffic
description:
Issue summary: WaveForms reports frequent 429 responses affecting a mixed workload of long-lived streaming chat sessions and periodic bulk embedding uploads. The customer suspects an interaction between token-slicing (per-connection allocation) and the dynamic refill algorithm that reduces burst credit when bulk uploads are active.

Impact: Several production customers see degraded throughput for chat users (increased reconnects) and intermittent failures for background embed jobs. Customer reports user-facing errors and job retries roughly every 5–15 minutes during peak windows.

Environment: Dedicated pool (customer-dedicated), prod-us-east, hybrid traffic: ~150 concurrent streaming sessions + 50 simultaneous batch embedding jobs at peak. API keys are scoped per service (chat vs ingest) and fronted by a multiplexing proxy.

Observed behavior: 1) Streaming sessions receive 429 with X-RateLimit headers showing near-zero available tokens for the minute window, while overall tenant usage in console shows spare credits in the hourly/burst pool. 2) Bulk uploads spike token consumption then drain quickly; after the spike, streaming sessions continue to hit minute-window 429s for ~30–90s despite refill.

Expected behavior: Streaming lanes should retain a steady small allotment and recover within the configured refill interval. Bulk ingestion should reduce its immediate burst impact through route isolation or separate burst pools so interactive connections are preserved.

Requested: Clarify how token-slicing (per-connection or per-route slices) interacts with the dynamic refill & burst smoothing logic, and provide configuration recommendations (route isolation, refill intervals and window sizes) for a mixed streaming+bulk workload on a dedicated pool.
steps_to_reproduce: 1) On a dedicated pool, configure two API keys: chat-key (long-lived streaming) and ingest-key (bulk uploads).
2) Start 150 concurrent streaming sessions using chat-key that keep an open SSE/websocket.
3) Launch 50 parallel embedding jobs via ingest-key that each upload batches (avg 2k tokens/job) over 30s windows.
4) Observe 429s in streaming sessions between 0s and 90s after bulk spike; check token/RateLimit headers and console quota graphs.
logs: [2026-03-10T14:02:11Z] upstream=rate-limiter decision=reject tenant=waveforms reason=minute_window_exhausted remaining=0 window=60s
investigation_notes:
Initial telemetry shows minute-window counters are tracked per connection slice when multiplexing/proxying is present. The ingest pipeline's parallelism is consuming many minute tokens across many short-lived connections, and the proxy's connection reuse is fragmenting refill credits (token-slicing) so interactive lanes get starved. We reproduced a similar pattern in staging by introducing a small parallel bulk fanout: minute window drops to zero even though hourly burst remains. Hypothesis: refill smoothing aggregates at the tenant layer but token accounting occurs at connection/route layer, causing transient misalignment.

Action taken: Captured pcap and rate-limit traces; flagged for SRE to review per-route burst pools and connection affinity settings. Asked engineering to validate whether the proxy preserves API key scoping or anonymizes connection identity causing slices to multiply.
workaround: Short-term: 1) Reduce ingest parallelism to spread batch uploads over a longer window (recommended: 5–10s inter-job jitter), 2) Configure separate route-level burst pool for ingest-key (request via support), or 3) Temporarily pin chat sessions to an isolated route that has a dedicated small burst allocation. We provided a sample config template to the customer for staggered backoff and per-route burst request.
resolution_notes: TBD - awaiting SRE analysis of proxy connection accounting. If confirmed, plan is: a) adjust proxy to preserve API-key->connection affinity, b) enable route isolation on dedicated pool for ingest vs chat, c) consider increasing minute-window size for interactive routes. Follow-up ticket(s) will include exact config changes and rollout plan.
